title: Breaking the Rules: Master the rules first, then break them with purpose
summary: Using Picasso's classical mastery and Volkswagen's "Lemon" ad, Jason Cohen argues that rules are reasonable defaults, not straightjackets. Breaking them works only when you understand them and do it deliberately. Innovation often comes from breaking a rule no one else will.

principles.text: Learn the rules first; mastery turns rule-breaking into a credible choice rather than incompetence.
principles.quote: Had Picasso never proven he could paint classically, he could be dismissed as a hack. When you know the rules, you're allowed to break the rules.

principles.text: No rule is unbreakable, provided you break it with purpose.
principles.quote: There's no rule that can't be broken, so long as it's broken with purpose.

principles.text: Treat rules as reasonable defaults when you have no better idea, not as a straightjacket.
principles.quote: Rules exist to guide us--a reasonable default when we don't have a better idea--but they're not a straightjacket.

principles.text: Inspired ideas often come from breaking a rule nobody else is willing to break.
principles.quote: In fact, the truly innovative, inspired ideas are frequently the result of breaking a rule that no one else is willing to break.

principles.text: Breaking a rule well requires calibration: grab attention without being so subtle the point is lost. Understanding the rule gets the balance right.
principles.quote: They played with words exactly enough to get your attention but not so subtly that you missed the point. Without appreciating the rule, the balance might not have been achieved.

principles.text: Break a rule without knowing it and you're probably just mistaken, not innovative.
principles.quote: But if you never bothered to learn the rules, you're probably just mistaken.
